newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Luxembourg and Greece show EMU opposites [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT].
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Luxembourg and Greece show EMU opposites [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT].

text.p: Greece and Luxembourg both gained 100 percent scores in a Reuters survey published Monday on how countries are shaping up for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- but at opposite ends of economists' expectations.
In the first quarterly survey of convergence criteria for EMU eligibility, all contributors predicted Luxembourg would meet all five entrance criteria for membership.
There was similar unanimity that Greece would fail to meet a single one of the criteria.

In a separate monthly survey plotting expectations of which of the 15 European Union countries would join EMU's first wave, all 41 of those polled expected Luxembourg to be included and none expected Greece to be.

Fiscal prudence and low cost pressures were cited as the reasons ensuring Luxembourg's membership, while Greece would have to wait until public finances were back on track and inflation had been subdued, the survey showed.

"In Luxembourg the government has always tried to moderate spending and the low level of indebtedness is due to this. Current and past governments have always tried to be careful," said Chimeno Raul, economist at Credit Suisse in Switzerland.

In Greece the opposite is true -- the government is still struggling to undo past profligacy and bring inflation back under control. Analysts say this is exacerabated by low growth rates and structural problems.
Headline inflation in Greece rose 8.3 percent year-on-year in October from 8.5 percent in September.
(Corrects to headline inflation from core inflation).
The average of 14 inflation forecasts in the Reuters quarterly survey was 6.9 percent averaged over 1997.

In Luxembourg, September consumer prices grew at 1.49 percent year-on-year and at 1.35 percent in August. The average of 15 forecasts from the quarterly survey showed analysts expected a rise of 2.0 percent year-on-year averaged over 1997.
The quarterly survey of convergence criteria questioned 34 economists across Europe who specialise in EMU affairs.

For Luxembourg, 20 out of 20 experts said they expected the budget deficit to be at or below three percent of GDP and total debt to be below 60 percent of GDP by the end of next year, as defined in the Maastricht Treaty.
By contrast, for Greece all 19 contributors in these categories expected the budget deficit to be 4.5 percent of GDP and for total debt to be over 70 percent of GDP by end-1997.

European Commission forecasts show Luxembourg's budget to be in surplus at 0.5 percent of GDP in 1997 and total debt at 8.8 percent of GDP by the end of next year. The Commission expects Greece's budget deficit for 1997 to be 6.5 percent of GDP and total debt to be over 110 percent of GDP.

In terms of keeping inflation and interest rates low during 1997, all who contributed predicted Luxembourg would meet the criteria. But only one of the 16 contributors expected Greece to keep inflation sufficiently under control and there was only one respondent predicting Greek interest rates to be low enough.
Robert Hayward, economic adviser at Bank of America pointed to the differences in the structural make-up of the two widely diverging economies.
"Luxembourg has the advantage of having a thriving financial services sector, reinforced by a favorable tax regime for investors," he said.
"Greece is still very dependent on agriculture and is struggling to make the structural changes necessary to bring it in line with European practices".
Attempts by the Greek government to liberalise the economy have not been completely successful and there is also a lot of resistance to change in Greece, analysts say.
Raul said: "Most businesses in Greece are small family-run firms, and the competition that followed from some of the de-regulation seems to have made the economic situation worse."
